data.title: Dražovce – a hillfort with the most photogenic church near Nitra
data.excerpt: The village of Dražovce lies 6 km west of Nitra, and above it, on the western spur of the Zobor range, stands one of the most photogenic small churches in Slovakia. The upper part of the hill was enclosed by ramparts and served as a hillfort; around the church people were buried for roughly 500 years, from the 11th century to the first half of the 17th century.
data.metaTitle: Dražovce – a hillfort with a famous church near Nitra
data.metaDescription: A famous small church stands on the hillfort above Dražovce near Nitra; a charter of Zobor Abbey of 1113 records the village as Villa Drasey S. Ypoliti.

keyFacts.label: Position
keyFacts.value: The village of Dražovce lies 6 km west of Nitra; the hillfort stands on a steep hill above the village, on the western spur of the Zobor range.

keyFacts.label: The Dražovce church
keyFacts.value: The hillfort is crowned by the well-known Dražovce church, which is among the most photogenic small churches in Slovakia.

keyFacts.label: Length of the summit rampart
keyFacts.value: The summit rampart is 190 m long and encloses the plateau of the acropolis in a great arc.

keyFacts.label: Area of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: According to Janšák’s survey the area of the hillfort was 4.2 ares.

keyFacts.label: Three enclosures of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: The hillfort had three enclosures – two outer baileys between the ramparts and one inner space, the acropolis preserved to this day.

keyFacts.label: Construction of the fortification
keyFacts.value: In the eastern part of the rampart the defensive wall consisted of two stone walls with a timber structure filled with earth; in the northern part there was probably only a timber palisade.

keyFacts.label: Centuries of burial
keyFacts.value: Burial went on in the cemetery by the church for roughly 500 years, from the 11th century to the first half of the 17th century.

keyFacts.label: Prehistoric occupation
keyFacts.value: Finds of pottery (the Lengyel culture, the Channelled Ware culture) show that the plateau was already occupied in prehistory, in the Neolithic.

children.text: The village of Dražovce lies close to Nitra, 6 km west of the city. The first record of the village of Dražovce has survived in a charter of Zobor Abbey of 1113, where it is recorded as "Villa Drasey S. Ypoliti". Above the village rises a steep hill — the western spur of the Zobor range — on which a small church stands. It is the well-known
Dražovce church

, which is among the most photogenic small churches in Slovakia. The first church, built of stone some time around the middle of the 11th century, has survived only in the foundations of the present building. The ground plan of the nave was the same as it is today; the apse, by contrast, originally had a horseshoe shape. The original building was destroyed and only its foundations survived. On them a new church was built in the next phase, again mostly of stone, with a small admixture of brick. After some time this one too was destroyed, and from it the walls survived to a height of 3 to 3.5 metres around the whole circuit, including the apse.

The present church, now of brick, was built making use of these walls — they are the upper part of the walls of the nave with three windows, the low superstructure of the apse and its vault, the conch. The rock is formed of Jurassic limestones. The upper part of the hill, enclosed by ramparts, served as a hillfort. On the eastern side of the hillfort a higher rampart has survived; on the southern side the rampart has mostly been destroyed by the quarrying of stone, because the place served as a quarry in the past. On the west the rock had such a slope that fortifications were probably not built here; on the northern side only smaller remains of the rampart are left. East of the first rampart ran two lower ramparts.

The hillfort was first surveyed and described by Š. Janšák. His detailed plan of the hillfort with contour lines and cross sections showed its state in 1929. A comparison of the plan with the state of the hillfort in 1947 shows that since that time the quarry has almost completely destroyed the rampart on the southern side. On the northern side the rampart, which ran at the very edge of the plateau, has disintegrated and largely collapsed. Š. Janšák states that there was a prehistoric hillfort here, and he describes in detail the composition of the larger rampart and the Christian cemetery, whose graves were partly sunk into the rampart. The area of the hillfort then measured 4.2 ares. The surface was considerably damaged by dug graves, more recent pits and the grazing of livestock, mainly pigs.

blocks.text: the natural safety of the hillfort is given by the fact that towards the north and the west the mountain spur descends very steeply into the valley, requiring no defence at all on the west and only a simple rampart on the north. The natural approach to the hillfort is from the southern side, from the village of Dražovce, up a gently rising slope. Of the artificial fortifications, only the line of the summit rampart can today be established with certainty, even though it is interrupted in two places. This rampart, 190 m long, encloses within itself in a great arc, on the southern, eastern and northern sides, a very convenient plateau, suitable to serve the function of an acropolis. Of the remaining outer ramparts, only rampart a b d, 160 m long, and b c, 44 m long, are discernible today, both ending on the eastern side at the points c, d. It is evident, however, that they continued further and enclosed two large baileys, which in their extent reached even to the ground where part of the village of Dražovce stands today. The summit rampart k l m n o p r is very much flattened, only about 80 cm high towards the interior of the hillfort. Towards the outside it ran above a steep step in the terrain, with which together it still forms a 3—4 m high obstacle even today. It is interrupted at the point p by an entrance which, judging by the overall situation of the hillfort and of its fortifications, may have been the original gateway into it. The material of which this rampart is made can be conveniently determined at the places interrupted by the quarry. In the section k l it is clay and sand scorched, and that by so fierce a heat that it yields slag entirely similar to the slag of blast furnaces. In its vicinity completely preserved charcoal is to be found in places. In the section m n, where the rampart is open for 18 m of its length, there occurs, beside burnt clay, a great quantity of grey ash (not charcoal) mixed with a negligible quantity of pottery sherds and with abundant fragments of flat stalactites, giving the impression of primitive implements of the first Stone Age. At the points n o, and further at several places on the surface (mainly on the northern side), strong traces of heat can again be established quite safely, which would point to the ramparts that the specialist literature calls “vitrified”. Rampart a b d runs towards the south-east and then in a great arc to the south, descending from spot height 204 to 183 and ending at the point d. In its upper section it is very distinct and gradually disappears. Parallel with it runs the remnant of rampart b c. Both of these ramparts, made of material without any traces of fire, are not closed off, they enclose nothing, nor do they join any natural obstacle, and they therefore logically require (in view of the analogy of other hillforts and of practical purpose) such a continuation that a certain space would be perfectly closed off by them. That is possible only if we imagine, on the western side, completely disturbed by the quarry, their junction by rampart e f as far as the rock, or to the summit rampart. This assumption is supported by the discovery of the remains of a vitrified rampart on the south-western side, immediately above the Gypsy (well now, Mr Janšák, such political incorrectness!) colony. The slope there is cut through by a clay pit and a quarry, and in one place there is ash, charcoal and burnt clay in it, about 1 m below the surface. From this it could be deduced that the hillfort had three enclosures: two outer ones, indicated by the segments between the ramparts a b d, b c, and one inner, the acropolis preserved to this day.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

children.text: Already in the 1920s, when Štefan Janšák surveyed the hillfort and carried out the first investigation on it, the state of preservation of the hillfort was alarming. Janšák describes it in these vivid terms:

blocks.text:
The attention of the present population is today drawn rather to the Christian cemetery, with its conspicuous remains of the buried persons and of the things buried with them, than to the old, prehistoric settlement. Unruly youngsters play merrily with whole skulls and shin bones, towards which not even the pigs behave with any reverence. The adults, for their part, collect weapons and small ornaments (all from the historical period) which found their way into the graves. According to oral information gathered on the spot, at least a considerable number of such objects is in the hands of several citizens of Dražovce.

Finds can be established with certainty only in the summit rampart, which also conceals the remains of the Christian burial ground. These are, as has already been mentioned, clay and sand burnt red, a quantity of ash mixed with sand, sherds which cannot be safely determined from the material obtained so far, and fragments of stalactites in the ash.
blocks.author: Štefan Janšák

children.text: Prehistoric occupation of the plateau

During the excavation of the hillfort it was established on the basis of the find material that it had already been occupied in prehistory. Individual prehistoric sherds and fragments of stone tools were found in the trenches and in the fill of the graves. A reddish bowl with straight walls can be assigned to the Neolithic; below its rim two oval knobs were placed vertically. Some fragments of pottery with plastic decoration also come from this period, for example a sherd with a horizontally placed lug, a sherd with a small conical projection, a cylindrical knob and a sherd decorated with deep grooves. Pottery made of grainy material of yellow or reddish colour most probably belonged to the sphere of the Lengyel culture. The Channelled Ware culture was represented by more distinctive remains. The flat clay spindle whorls, fragments of flint tools and cores dug up on the area of the hillfort were in use in the Neolithic and in the Eneolithic, so their dating cannot be decided with certainty. Besides sherds, the remains of a dwelling were also discovered, which probably also belonged to the Channelled Ware culture.
The fortification of the hillfort

children.text: The first, larger rampart was investigated at two places. The trench dug in the eastern stretch of the rampart showed that the rampart had been disturbed by more recent graves, so it was not possible to reconstruct its whole section here. In the eastern slope of the rampart, at a depth of 30 cm, a layer of ash began; it was mixed with charcoal and burnt stones and went down to a depth of 80 cm onto the bedrock. Behind the layer of ash there was in the rampart a 35 cm thick layer of red burnt clay; it began at a depth of 30 cm.

The trench in the north-eastern part of the rampart yielded a better preserved section, and it was established that two stone walls, drystone-laid, ran along the sides of the rampart. The layer of stone on the northern side was 60 cm high and 130 cm wide. The stone wall on the southern side was 35 cm high and 140 cm wide, and the distance between them was 430 cm.

On the basis of the sections through the rampart a reconstruction of the fortification can be made. In the eastern part of the rampart the defensive wall consisted of two stone walls, between which there was a timber structure filled with earth. Of interest is the use of a wedge-shaped support to strengthen the wall at the bend, where the wall might most easily have collapsed. In the northern part of the rampart there was probably only a timber palisade, of which a layer of black earth with charcoal has remained. This part of the fortification also had a more recent phase, in which a rampart of earth from the area of the burial ground was heaped onto the layer of black earth.

children.text: Kraskovská also states that the construction of the fortification follows on from the ramparts of the Great Moravian period. The favourable position of the hillfort and the proximity of the Nitra agglomeration suggest that it was built and used already in the time of Great Moravia. Its position positively invites the building here of at least a guard hillfort with a predominantly military function. The construction of the defensive wall likewise suggests that it could have been built in the period of Great Moravia (a timber-and-earth structure with a small stone wall). Unfortunately, the excavation did not succeed in unambiguously documenting the existence of a magnate’s residence from the time of Great Moravia, because the hillfort lacks finds that would indicate the presence of a wealthy stratum. No foundations or remains of a representative building were found, nor any luxury goods from this period – as was the case, for example, at Ducové. In his opinion, however, such an absence of finds can be explained by the fact that the whole presumed occupation layer of the 9th century was devastated in the course of antiquity by the permanent use of the hillfort area as a burial ground, where older graves were often destroyed by newer ones. At the same time it may be assumed that the 9th-century layer was destroyed already by the oldest graves of the 11th century.
(note by Orgoň)
The medieval burial ground

blocks.caption: Štefan Janšák surveyed and drew the hillfort before it was partly damaged by the quarry
blocks.alt: Štefan Janšák surveyed and drew the hillfort before it was partly damaged by the quarry

children.text:
The number of graves found in the area suggests that already in the 11th century the place began to serve as a cemetery. During the time of burial the place evidently lost its function as a hillfort. The objects found testify to the continuous use of the cemetery from the 11th century to the first half of the 17th century, that is, through almost the whole feudal era. Burial went on in the cemetery by the church for roughly 500 years in a relatively small area, so older graves were constantly being disturbed and the ground around the church was dug over completely. No coherent groups from individual periods remained in the cemetery. The items of clothing found in the cemetery supplement our modest insights into the dress of the rural population, especially in the 14th and 15th centuries. The dress included leather belts with bronze and bone ornaments. The wide sleeves of women’s garments were gathered with narrow leather straps with bronze ornaments. Items of rich dress (belts, finger rings) show that some of the buried persons belonged to the feudal gentry. The burial ground at Dražovce provided indisputable evidence that the custom of placing coins in the grave survived here through the whole Middle Ages and still lasted in the first half of the 17th century. Likewise the custom of placing knives in the grave was verified for the 16th century by a coin.
 
 Present state and marking: about 100 metres from the hillfort, at the start of a field track in front of a barrier, you can leave the car, and at the barrier an exemplary information panel informs you not only about the
church
, but also about the Slavic hillfort. The only pity is perhaps that the
church
is not usually open.
